location.description: The location for which to retrieve the weather forecast, in the format of 'City, Country' (e.g., 'London, UK').

start_date.description: The start date for the forecast period in the format of 'YYYY-MM-DD' (e.g., '2023-04-01').

end_date.description: The end date for the forecast period in the format of 'YYYY-MM-DD' (e.g., '2023-04-07').

include_details.description: Whether to include detailed hourly forecast data or not. If set to false, only daily summaries will be provided.

message.content:
The sea usually looks **blue**—but that’s just the most common hue you’ll notice when you look out over open water. The reason is that water absorbs longer wavelengths (reds, oranges, yellows) more strongly than shorter wavelengths (blues). The remaining blue light is scattered in all directions by the water molecules and tiny particles, so our eyes perceive a blue tint.

That said, the “color” of the sea can change depending on a few factors:

| Factor | Effect on Color |
|--------|-----------------|
| **Depth** | Deeper water tends to appear darker blue or even greenish‑black because more light is absorbed. |
| **Algae & phytoplankton** | High concentrations give the water a greenish or turquoise tint. |
| **Sediment & runoff** | Suspended silt or clay can make the water brownish or murky. |
| **Sun angle & weather** | Low sun angles (sunrise/sunset) can cast warm hues (orange, pink), while overcast skies can make the sea look grayish. |
| **Reflection** | Reflections of the sky, clouds, or nearby land can alter the perceived color. |

So while “blue” is the classic answer, the sea’s appearance is actually a dynamic blend of physics, biology, and environment.
